title: Algorithm Awareness: Why Am I Seeing This?
goal: Your kid finds out why YouTube and streaming apps show them what they show. They notice their recommendations, track what they watch for a few days, run a small experiment to see the suggestions change, spot the tricks that keep them watching, and choose what they'll watch on purpose.
need: The apps your family already uses, like YouTube or Netflix
Their own profile, a supervised account or YouTube Kids (YouTube accounts are 13+)
A notebook to track what they watch and what's suggested
Their usual screen time, nothing extra

academics.subject: Science
academics.text: a real experiment with a prediction

academics.subject: Thinking
academics.text: who decides what you see, and why

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: The trap is lecturing about screens. Your job is to get curious with them about how the app decides, run the experiment together, and let them discover the tricks for themselves.

plan.what: Notice and track their suggestions (Steps 1 and 2).
Spot the tricks and choose (Steps 4 and 5).

troubleshoot.q: The experiment uses up their screen time
troubleshoot.a: Use their usual time, not extra. A few searches and a look at the home page is enough.

troubleshoot.q: They share an account with a sibling
troubleshoot.a: Great for the experiment: compare what each person's watching does to the shared suggestions.
Keep it light. Knowing how the app works puts them back in charge; it's a superpower, not a scandal.

lesson.text: Apps like YouTube and Netflix use an algorithm: a program that learns from what you watch, how long you watch, and what people like you watch, then guesses what will keep you watching. Its job is to keep you watching. Knowing that is how you stay the one who decides.
lesson.before: 'The app just shows me what's good.'

model.line: Just one more video, all the time.
Picking his own videos instead of autoplay.

lesson.modelNote: The app learns what you like and serves more of it. Picking the next video yourself keeps the decision yours, not the app's.

steps.title: Notice what's suggested
steps.why: Lots of kids think the home page is the same for everyone. It isn't.
steps.kid: Your kid opens the app they use most and looks at the home page and the suggestions, using the What am I seeing? card in the Algorithm Toolkit at the end of the guide, and says why they think each one is there.
steps.you: Open the same app on your account, side by side. Compare: why is yours different?
ask: Why do you think this video is here?
Is your home page the same as mine?
steps.tip: Two accounts side by side is the fastest way to see that the app chooses differently for each person.

levels.explore: Point to three suggestions, and say if you've watched something like them before.
levels.develop: List the top ten suggestions, and guess why each one is there.
levels.extend: Find the 'Because you watched' or 'Up next' reason for three suggestions, and check if it's right.

steps.title: Track it for a few days
steps.why: Writing down what you watch and what's suggested shows the pattern the app is following.
steps.kid: For three days, your kid notes what they watched and the first three things suggested after, using the Track it card.
steps.you: Keep it quick: one line a day, during their usual screen time.
ask: What did the app show you next?
steps.tip: Look for the same topic coming back, again and again. That's the algorithm at work.

levels.explore: Each day, say what you watched and one thing it showed you after.
levels.develop: Track three days, and circle the suggestions that match what you watched.
levels.extend: Track a week, and count what share of suggestions matched your last video.

steps.title: Run an experiment
steps.why: Changing what you watch, on purpose, proves the app is following you.
steps.kid: Your kid picks a new topic, like a craft, an animal or a sport, watches or searches a few videos about it, then checks the home page again, using the Experiment card.
steps.you: Help them predict first: 'How many will be about the new topic tomorrow?' Then check together.
ask: What do you think will change?
How fast did the app change its suggestions?
steps.tip: Predict, then check. That's what makes it a real experiment.

levels.explore: Search one new thing, and see if it shows up on the home page.
levels.develop: Watch a new topic, predict the change, and count what changed the next day.
levels.extend: Then try to undo it: remove those videos from your watch history, and see how long the topic takes to fade.

steps.title: Spot the tricks
steps.why: Apps are designed to keep you watching. Seeing the design makes it easier to stop.
steps.kid: Your kid looks for the tricks on the Keep-you-watching tricks card, like autoplay, a countdown to the next video or endless scrolling, and marks the ones their app uses.
steps.you: Share the one that gets you, too. 'Just one more' happens to grown-ups as well.
ask: Which trick works best on you?
When does 'one more video' happen most?
steps.tip: Most tricks have an off switch, like turning autoplay off. Find them together.

levels.explore: Find one trick, like the next video starting by itself.
levels.develop: Find three tricks in your app, and how to turn them off.
levels.extend: Compare two apps, and decide which one tries harder to keep you watching.

steps.title: Choose on purpose
steps.why: Knowing how it works means they can decide what to watch, not the app.
steps.kid: Your kid picks two or three moves from the Take back control card, like choosing videos before opening the app or keeping autoplay off, and tries them for a week.
steps.you: Work inside the family limits you already have. This step is about what they watch, not how long.
ask: What will you watch, before you open the app?
Which suggestion was hardest to ignore?
steps.tip: Deciding what to watch before opening the app is the strongest move there is.

levels.explore: Choose your video before you open the app, with a parent.
levels.develop: Try two control moves for a week, and say which one helped.
levels.extend: Design a 'watch on purpose' plan for the family, and test it for a week.

skills.name: Algorithm awareness
skills.text: how apps choose what you see

conclusion.headline: They know why the app shows them what it shows.
conclusion.text: Watch the end of a video. If they reach past the countdown and pick the next one themselves, they've seen the algorithm at work and decided anyway.
conclusion.celebrate: When they pick the next video themselves instead of letting it autoplay, say: 'You chose that one, not the app.'
extensions: Run the experiment on a parent's account, with permission, and compare
Watch the same video on a guest profile, and compare the Up next list with yours
Look up how a streaming app decides what to suggest, in its own help pages
Notice suggestions in other places, like online shops and music apps

signs: They explain why a video was suggested to them
They pick what to watch before opening the app
They notice when a suggestion is pulling them in, and say so
makeItReal: This week, before anyone opens YouTube or a streaming app, ask them to say what they'll watch. Then check together whether they watched it, or what the app picked instead.

fromHome.text: My son mostly watches Minecraft videos on YouTube, and both kids have noticed their suggestions following what they watch. 'Just one more video' happens all the time. He picks his videos himself instead of letting autoplay choose.
